narrativeProgression.description: Interviewer poses the question about the cost of lawsuits.
Interviewee clarifies the misconception about court costs, emphasizing that lawyers' fees are the primary expense.
He explains the fixed nature of legal expenses as outlined in the British Columbia Civil Rules.
He contrasts legal expenses with lawyers' fees, which are negotiable.
He provides specific examples of court costs to illustrate their affordability.
He suggests that individuals need to understand legal procedures to manage costs effectively.
He emphasizes that learning about legal procedures can help mitigate costs.
He acknowledges the need for legal expertise in some cases but encourages individuals to become informed about the legal process.
He differentiates between fixed and malleable legal rules.
He suggests that as cases become more complex, a mix of fixed, malleable, and improvised rules might come into play.
He emphasizes that lawyers undergo formal training, while clients do not.
He stresses the importance of client education and informed decision-making in managing legal costs.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Keep we know that lawsuits are very expensive. How is your society dealing with costs?
People often say that it's very expensive to go to court. It's actually not. It's actually
quite cheap to go to court. It's the lawyers that are expensive. Actual legal expenses
are set out in appendix C, schedule one, or the back of the British Columbia civil
rules. And in there, it lays out what the actual legal expenses are. And their legal expenses
because they're set out in statute. You can't negotiate them in general. You have to
pay them. However, they're not very expensive. To bring a multi-million dollar suit, you're
looking at $200 to file. It's $80 to file a requisition. $200 to set down a trial date.
What you're actually hearing about when people say legal expenses, they're really talking
about contractor fees. In other words, lawyers fees. And those are totally different than
what the court expects. The contractor fees are not legal fees. They're what someone
believes that they're entitled to. We have to make decisions every day on how to manage
and instruct counsel appropriately. We understand how to responsibly give instructions. We understand
what the options are ahead of us and what the consequences are at each step of the way.
One of the ways that we're able to mitigate is by learning the civil procedures on our
own because the courts are ultimately a public utility. And to a certain extent, unfortunately,
people do have to rent access to powers of comprehension over laws that were intended
to be public utilities. But there's nothing to stop people who are not lawyers from reading
the civil procedures. There's many books written on them. We have the civil rules. In my
space as an engineer, I have to deal with much more complicated technical documents on
a daily basis that are not subjective in nature. They're not malleable. They're not subject
to the powers of persuasion. They're set in stone. Law is different in that respect
in that. There's sort of three categories of rules. There's rules that are set in stone,
like the statute of limitations. There's rules that are malleable, like the rules of evidence,
and then there's some rules that are just made up as they go along. And as things get
more complicated in proceeding, it's not unusual to see all of the three come out. Lawyers
have to go to law school to learn how to be your lawyer, but clients do not undertake
any type of training to learn how to be clients. And that's important because ultimately, you're
managing lawyers and your managerial skills are only as effective so far as you are informed
about the process.
